We used an automated evaluation to measure the efficacy of selected production moderation checks for the GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst and GPT-Image-2.6 Flare models.
We evaluated saved generations from a shared set of 3,077 challenging requests designed to generate images that would violate our policy across safety categories such as violence and sexual content.
Each model was compared with its corresponding GPT-Image-2.5 baseline using a common reference-grading procedure.
These results are not representative of how often violative requests or outputs arise in production traffic.
Each model and generation setting was evaluated on the same 3,077 requests.
Total Prompts: Total prompts meant to generate violative images as part of our automated evaluation process.
Safe Generation: Images where the adversarial prompt resulted in a non-violative image generation, whether or not the evaluated moderation checks would allow the image.
Unsafe Generation Blocked: Images where the adversarial prompt resulted in a violative image generation that was blocked by the evaluated moderation checks.
Unsafe Generation Not Blocked: Outputs graded violative that were not blocked by the evaluated moderation checks. This is an offline evaluation outcome, not observed delivery to users.

We find that the GPT-Images-2.6 series with moderation checks generally performs on par with GPT Images-2.5.

The other category includes long-tail categories that should be protected against including religious figures, religious satire, fabricated or compromising depictions of real people, jailbreak attempts, and image-based requests.
For the evaluated configurations shown, Sunburst produced fewer violative images post-moderation than its corresponding GPT-Images-2.5 baseline.
Flare’s rate increased from 1.49% (46 of 3,077 requests) to 2.14% (66 of 3,077), an increase of 0.65 percentage points. Neither overall difference was statistically significant.

Before moderation, the proportion of Flare outputs graded non-violative decreased from 78.36% to 75.04%. This decline was statistically significant, with the largest contributions coming from the “Other” and sexual prompt categories.
Of the 20 net additional unsafe outputs that were not blocked, 14 were in the “Other” category.
No individual prompt category showed a statistically significant increase in violative outputs when safety moderation was applied.

These evaluations use a fixed set of adversarial requests that are designed around challenging edge cases with automated grading. Results apply to the model and safeguard configurations evaluated and do not measure the complete deployed safety system or the frequency of violative outputs in production.
Upstream, LLM-based policy checks are designed to block potentially violative image requests before image generation begins.

Downstream Blocking: After a request reaches the image generation system, we use a safety reasoning model as a monitor to moderate both image inputs to the image generation model and the generated output.
We evaluated these safeguards using a targeted set of adversarial GIFs labeled as policy-violating.
The results indicate that neither GPT-Image-2.6 Sunburst nor GPT-Image-2.6 Flare cross the Bio High threshold or the Cyber High threshold.
